desc:
The array nums is circular: after the last element comes the first again. A circular subarray starts at any index and takes consecutive elements, wrapping around the end if needed, without using an index twice. It must contain at least 1 and at most k elements.

Return the largest sum of such a circular subarray.

Examples: for nums = [5, -3, 5], k = 2 the answer is 10 (the two fives, which are neighbours around the end); with k = 1 it is 5; with k = 3 it is 10 as well, because adding the -3 cannot help. For [-2, -3, -1] and k = 2 the answer is -1.
hints: Unroll the circle: a wrapping subarray is an ordinary subarray of nums + nums that starts in the first copy.
With prefix sums P of the doubled array, a subarray (s, e] has sum P[e] - P[s]. For each end e, you want the smallest P[s] among the allowed starts s ∈ [e-k, e-1].

A sliding-window minimum answers this in amortised O(1): keep a deque of indices whose prefix sums are increasing, drop indices that fell out of the window from the front, and drop larger values from the back before pushing the new one.
editorial: Concatenate the array with itself so wrapping subarrays become ordinary ones, and build prefix sums P of length 2n + 1. A subarray of length between 1 and k ending at doubled position e (exclusive) has sum P[e] - P[s] with e - k ≤ s ≤ e - 1. Because k ≤ n, no index is ever used twice, and any circular subarray appears with its start in the first copy.

For each e from 1 to 2n we need the minimum P[s] over a window of the last k prefix positions. That is the classic sliding-window minimum: a monotonic deque stores candidate indices with increasing P. Pop from the front when the index leaves the window, pop from the back while the back's value is not smaller than the new one, then the front is the minimum. Overall O(n) time and O(n) space. A direct double loop is O(n · k).
